title: Steam
description: Steam is water vapor released where heat meets colder air: trains, manholes, showers, a white veil that rises and thins. It is wet matter, not combustion; it billows, condenses on lens and wool, and has a thermal source.

sections.title: Narrative function

blocks.text: A locomotive writes a column that the platform wind tears. A manhole breathes.
A shower erases a body in white. Heat meeting cold air.
Industrial or intimate, the physics are the same. Use it when the source is hot water or hot metal in cold space.
It is the wrong tool when the cloud is burning (Smoke) or hanging as weather (Fog). Smoke can sink and stain; steam wants to rise and vanish.
If the white cloud has no grate, kettle, train, or shower, you have fog in a trench coat.

sections.title: How it works

blocks.text: Show the source (stack, manhole, shower head, kettle). Let the vapor rise and shear in wind.
Backlight for a white, translucent volume; it should feel wetter and brighter than smoke. Condensation on glass and wool helps.
Prompt: steam billowing around [Subject], trains, manholes, showers, a white veil, industrial or intimate heat.

sections.title: When to use it

blocks.text: Use it on a winter platform, a night street grate, a bathroom, a factory press. Do not use it as generic alley 'atmosphere' with no heat.
If the alley is burning, use smoke. If the alley is only wet and cold, use fog or rain.

sections.title: Compared with similar shots

blocks.text: Smoke is combustion, often grey or colored, with a fire source. Fog is ambient water droplets without a hot origin.
Atmospheric Haze is distant scatter. Steam is a thermal event: white, rising, local to a grate, stack, or shower.

sections.title: In film

blocks.text: Winter station grammar in thrillers leans on locomotive steam as moving architecture. The Untouchables uses train steam as a white, violent veil.
Drive lets night streets breathe from grates. Spirited Away treats bathhouse steam as a wet interior weather.
Show the heat, not a smoke bomb.

sections.title: What usually goes wrong

blocks.text: The usual wrong cousin is Smoke (wrong color, wrong source) or Fog (no rise from heat). The tell: a grey cloud sitting still with no grate or stack.
The fix: a thermal source, white translucent rise, backlight, wind shear.

sections.title: Questions

blocks.text: What is Steam in film?
Steam is water vapor from heat meeting colder air. It billows from trains, manholes, showers, and kettles: a white, wet, rising veil with a thermal source.
Steam vs Smoke
Smoke is combustion particles and can hang, stain, and go grey. Steam is wet vapor, brighter, rising, tied to heat and cold air. One burns; the other boils.
When should I use Steam?
Use it when heat and cold air are in the scene: platforms, grates, baths, presses. Do not use it as a generic alley cloud with no source.
How do I prompt Steam for AI image or video?
Name the hot source and the white rise. Example: steam billowing around [Subject], trains, manholes, showers, a white veil. Backlight it and keep it wetter than smoke.
